item.title: UNDP and FLock.io strengthen relationship to advance public sector digital innovation in the Dominican Republic
item.dc:creator: Marco Callegari
item.description:
FLock.io, a leading privacy-preserving AI solution provider, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have strengthened their relationship to advance public sector digital innovation for the Dominican Republic, building on an ongoing pilot this year. They have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to align with the UNDP Strategic Plan (2026–2029) to leverage new technologies […]

The post UNDP and FLock.io strengthen relationship to advance public sector digital innovation in the Dominican Republic appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
FLock.io, a leading privacy-preserving AI solution provider, and the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) have strengthened their relationship to advance public sector digital innovation for the Dominican Republic, building on an ongoing pilot this year. They have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to align with the UNDP Strategic Plan (2026–2029) to leverage new technologies for public service delivery and data-driven solutions while striving towards prosperity for all, including climate action and gender equality.

FLock.io led cohort 2 of pilots of the SDG Blockchain Accelerator – an initiative by the UNDP AltFin Lab team to scale practical solutions powered by AI and blockchain for sustainable development worldwide – in regions including the Caribbean, Liberia, Rwanda and Latin America, with cohort 3 to follow. In May, FLock.io visited the Dominican Republic to advance one such project: crop microinsurance to deliver payouts for damaged crops (which was previously unavailable to smallholder farmers) that combine AI-powered risk assessment with instant blockchain-based payouts. The team heard directly from local female farmers about the challenges they face. This is one example of FLock.io’s privacy-preserving AI and blockchain technology that doesn’t expose raw or sensitive data.

The Dominican Republic has witnessed a significant surge in digital adoption in recent years, with internet penetration now reaching 91% of the population. Emerging technologies have created unprecedented opportunities to transform the public sector, but to ensure it serves all citizens fairly it requires strong data privacy standards and ethical governance frameworks. Bridging these gaps requires human-centered, privacy-preserving infrastructure.

The MoU marks a key milestone in FLock.io’s engagement with UNDP Dominican Republic. Under this framework agreement signed on September 4, 2026, FLock.io and the UNDP Country Office in the Dominican Republic will collaborate on knowledge exchange, dialogue and institutional learning. The effort supports the UNDP Country Programme Document for the Dominican Republic (2023–2027) and the UNDP Strategic Plan (2026–2029) by exploring responsible public infrastructure, transparent data governance and trusted public systems that enable governments to drive innovation while maintaining control over local data and upholding ethics. The dialogue will focus on strengthening inclusive digital systems, supporting gender-responsive social protection systems, and climate and environmental sustainability.

This collaboration builds on FLock.io’s growing engagement with governments and public institutions. After a successful pilot with the government of Sarawak, Malaysia, FLock.io was announced as the key technical partner in a sovereign AI government initiative and signed three landmark MoUs during a series of UK-Sarawak strategic roundtables in Manchester, Cambridge then Oxford.

item.title: Why small businesses could be the big winners from AI
item.dc:creator: Marco Callegari
item.description:
Attributed to Ruchi Sharma, Vice President, UK Commercial at American Express Do small businesses risk getting left behind by the rise of AI? Or are they fuelling a growing wave of adoption as they embrace the opportunity it offers? Small businesses tend to have less time and budget to adopt new technologies than larger firms. […]

The post Why small businesses could be the big winners from AI appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
Attributed to Ruchi Sharma, Vice President, UK Commercial at American Express

Do small businesses risk getting left behind by the rise of AI? Or are they fuelling a growing wave of adoption as they embrace the opportunity it offers?

Small businesses tend to have less time and budget to adopt new technologies than larger firms. And while the Government’s own research shows the same early gap in AI adoption, the trend may play out differently in this new era – with the potential for AI to power small business growth.

Lack of time is the biggest barrier to growth

AI is not just popular with SME owners because the tools are so accessible. It also gives owners something immensely valuable: time.

Running a small business requires serious hard work and dedication, with entrepreneurs often working long hours to ensure their business survives and thrives. But it often means they’re spread thin across multiple responsibilities – with limited time to focus on growth.

American Express’ annual Business Barometer research, released last month, found that more than a third (36%) of the SME owners surveyed cited their own lack of capacity as the single biggest barrier to growing their business – with much of that capacity lost to routine work. These entrepreneurs said they spend an average of 11 hours per week on administrative or finance-related tasks, roughly six working days a month that could go on growth.

More than a time-saver

The data shows that there’s a clear and critical need amongst business owners to carve out more time for growth, and they’re already turning to AI to win that time back.

Four in five (83%) are using AI in some form and many see it as a practical way to offload routine tasks, and one in five (21%) would go so far as to say that AI is like having another member of staff.

When I speak to small business owners, this comes up again and again. AI has not replaced their judgement or creativity, it has amplified their capacity, letting founders and small teams operate at a level that used to require a far larger team.

It is not just about saving time. For entrepreneurs, who are often making decisions on their own or solving unfamiliar problems, AI tools are providing a valuable source of information. Among those already using AI, nearly a third (29%) say they have used it to learn new skills or get business advice.

But adoption is still in relative infancy, with nearly one in five (18%) saying AI still feels like a blind spot they know they should be making more of.

Powering the UK’s small business economy

Evidently, there is still a fair way to go to grow AI adoption and unlock this opportunity for small businesses. But the implication of this data is still significant. SMEs are the backbone of the UK economy, and with AI adoption in relative infancy, this presents an important opportunity for small businesses to boost their own productivity and growth – and that of the wider economy.

At American Express, we are committed to backing small businesses – that is why earlier this year, we launched an AI training initiative with non-profit Generation, to help small firms build practical AI skills in their day-to-day operations.

Small business owners are some of the most resourceful and ambitious people I meet. AI gives them the opportunity to turn that resourcefulness into even greater impact. The question, then, is not whether small businesses will be left behind by AI, but how quickly we can help more of them seize its potential. If we get that right, the prize will be bigger than more productive businesses: it will be a stronger, more dynamic UK economy.

item.dc:creator: Marco Callegari
item.description:

The life sciences company has developed VivoScan™, a high-throughput screening platform that uses C. elegans nematode worms to test potential drug candidates in a whole organism. Magnitude combines the worms with imaging, machine learning, […]

The post Magnitude Biosciences raises £1.3m to scale drug discovery platform appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
Durham University spinout Magnitude Biosciences has raised £1.3m to scale its drug discovery platform and expand its work with pharmaceutical companies.

The life sciences company has developed VivoScan™, a high-throughput screening platform that uses C. elegans nematode worms to test potential drug candidates in a whole organism.

Magnitude combines the worms with imaging, machine learning, AI, automation and robotics to generate biological data on potential treatments.

The company said the technology can allow pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies to screen drug candidates more quickly and cheaply than conventional approaches, with an initial focus on ageing, longevity and neurodegenerative diseases.

Northstar Ventures led the £1.3m funding round, investing through the North East Spinout Inspire Fund, North East Innovation Fund and Northstar EIS Growth Fund.

Maven-managed regional funds also participated, including NPIF II – Maven Equity Finance and the Finance Durham Fund, alongside new angel investors.

The investment will also enable Magnitude Biosciences to access a £217,000 Innovate UK Investor Partnership grant.

Magnitude plans to use the capital to expand VivoScan, increase its commercial activity with global pharmaceutical companies, invest in equipment and automation and recruit additional staff.

The company ultimately wants VivoScan to be capable of screening millions of compounds using whole-organism models.

Dr Fozia Saleem, CEO of Magnitude Biosciences, said: “Our ambition is to become the first company to provide a platform to screen millions of compounds in a whole organism.

“This investment in VivoScan™ gives us the opportunity to turn that ambition into reality and fundamentally change the scale and speed at which drug discovery can be done.

“We are building a platform that can move beyond simply screening more compounds. VivoScan™ generates rich, whole-organism biological data that can help researchers understand how potential therapies affect health, ageing and disease.”

The investment comes amid efforts across the pharmaceutical industry to find alternatives to traditional mammalian testing and reduce the time and cost involved in identifying viable drug candidates.

Magnitude Biosciences was spun out of Durham University and operates as a contract research organisation, providing drug discovery services to pharmaceutical and biotechnology businesses.

The £22.5m North East Spinout Inspire Fund, which participated in the round, is backed by Durham, Newcastle, Northumbria, Sunderland and Teesside universities and the North East Mayoral Strategic Authority. It was established to invest in companies commercialising research originating from the region’s universities.

Dr Will Cousins, investment manager at Northstar Ventures, said: “Having worked closely with Magnitude Biosciences throughout its journey, we have seen first-hand the strength of the team, the technology and the opportunity ahead.

“We are proud to continue backing a business that is helping to shape the future of drug discovery.”

Sarah Newbould, senior investment manager at the British Business Bank, added: “We’re continuing to back the businesses that are driving innovation across the UK economy, with this new funding round helping to bring Magnitude Biosciences’ new technology to market.”

item.title: Adapting energy data access for other markets
item.dc:creator: Marco Callegari
item.description:
By Paul Linnane, Chief Data Officer, ElectraLink For a select few energy market devotees, energy data has been available for the past 10 years and a number of highly successful companies have been leveraging it to improve the sector. More recently, a massive transformation is occurring in the UK energy market and its data-sharing ecosystem […]

The post Adapting energy data access for other markets appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
By Paul Linnane, Chief Data Officer, ElectraLink

For a select few energy market devotees, energy data has been available for the past 10 years and a number of highly successful companies have been leveraging it to improve the sector. More recently, a massive transformation is occurring in the UK energy market and its data-sharing ecosystem to make data more visible to a wider group of participants. However, after attending PropTech Connect in London recently, I was keenly reminded that, unless you work in data operations or governance within an energy business, most people in organisations that interact with energy data don’t need to know the details of the Market-wide Half Hourly Settlement (MHHS) programme, nor the DSI, CSS, DCC or CCS. This is just “inside baseball,” to use an American term.

The programme becomes relevant for folks from other sectors when considering how tech enablers are adapting their approaches and systems to a new world of data sharing. Energy data was once confined to closed systems to serve a small number of energy-related purposes. However, organisations like ElectraLink have leveraged historical connections to unlock energy data for any organisation that can meet governance requirements and has a sustainable business model that harnesses data-driven processes.

Precedent in unlocking energy data

For years, retail energy market data was rarely used outside of the energy sector and as such the focus was on usage and bills. Now that whole-system decarbonisation is mature, and digitalisation is endemic across almost all customer journeys, organisations have found a widening array of valuable uses of this data.

ElectraLink has been contributing to this for at least 13 years. We initially aimed to make energy – particularly usage – data accessible to enhance competition and lower barriers to entry (and costs) within the retail energy market. The data we have offered for that time has come from the regulated, centralised arm of ElectraLink’s business – the Data Transfer Service (DTS) – which is mandated by industry rules to transfer data between electricity networks, suppliers and metering agents. ElectraLink was given permission to copy and store all the data flowing across the DTS for the benefit of households and businesses as energy innovation matures, especially since the smart meter rollout started in 2011.

Access to this data and a solid governance model has enabled the development of a range of services. With data solutions like QuoteRight and MeterReader integrated via API, and file transfer solutions like 5Sites, a mix of business models have been empowered to digitalise processes for end user convenience and decarbonisation journeys.

ElectraLink also has a strong relationship with the UK Government through our provision of EMPRIS – an energy data insights platform – to the Department of Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which uses the data to understand trends and outcomes for end consumers. Our existing ties with DESNZ have served as useful avenues to learn and test new use cases for the data we hold, alongside building a reputation that supports early access to valuable data.

With many successful projects and collaborations on our books, we have since expanded into other industries, such as banking, real estate, tech and sustainability.

ElectraLink and its brilliant data experts are now adapting to changes emerging from the MHHS programme. This will ensure data access continues and improves for businesses looking for a competitive edge.

Extending access through new and old relationships

In a few years’ time, once the MHHS programme is complete, there will be more data than ever providing granular insights into energy usage behaviours for every home and business premises in Great Britain.

However, like with any transition, the bit in the middle is messy. To support our customers and ensure this data remained accessible as the data moved home, ElectraLink worked with central players in the energy market and signed agreements to collaborate to continue to make this huge volume of data available through our systems. In this way, the effects of digital transformation on our customers are minimised and improved.

Again, at various conferences we are reminded that for those outside energy there is always a need for diligent organisations to navigate the governance, access, technical jargon and make it easy for other sectors to add the data to their value stack. The more this happens, the greater impact the energy digitisation will have on end consumers, whether that be the tariff of their bill, the performance of their home battery, the interest rate they pay on their mortgage or comfort of the building that they work in.

Opening access to energy data provides opportunities for new business models and propositions. From understanding energy usage habits, homeowners can reduce their bills and contribute to flexibility schemes. Businesses can calculate and reduce their carbon emissions, upgrade their facilities with industrial-scale, low-carbon technologies and buy energy further in advance at lower prices. This data also helps with valuing real estate assets as well as modelling risk on loans and mortgages with green finance features.

Adopt early and lead

With this data now available on a commercial basis, being the first to access it is critical to moving ahead of the competition. We have seen in many industries how those who tap in early become leaders in their own right – it is no different with energy data.

While a little known but widely consequential digital transformation programme had the potential to squeeze existing data availability, ElectraLink has improved the types of data on offer that can be surfaced for customer-facing apps and interfaces as well as consultancy-level reporting and insights.

The post Adapting energy data access for other markets appeared first on UKTN.

item.title: First Table raises $12 million NZD to fuel expansion across the UK and Ireland
item.dc:creator: Marco Callegari
item.description:
First Table, the restaurant booking platform that gives diners 50% off their food bill for dining at an off-peak time while helping restaurants fill empty tables, has raised $12 million NZD to fund its next phase of growth, with the UK and Ireland at the centre of the strategy. The round was backed by existing […]

The post First Table raises $12 million NZD to fuel expansion across the UK and Ireland appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
First Table, the restaurant booking platform that gives diners 50% off their food bill for dining at an off-peak time while helping restaurants fill empty tables, has raised $12 million NZD to fund its next phase of growth, with the UK and Ireland at the centre of the strategy.

The round was backed by existing investors Altered Capital, Invest South, Mainland Angels and Snowball Effect shareholders, alongside new investors K1W1 and Icehouse Ventures.

The UK has emerged as First Table’s standout market, with bookings growing over 150% year on year and London now the company’s busiest city globally. Since entering the market, First Table has expanded rapidly across the UK and Ireland, launching in 22 cities to date,more than 10 of them in the past year alone, and building a network of over 2,000 restaurant partners across the two countries.

“The First Table model travels. 50% off your food bill is appealing no matter where in the world you are,” said CEO Alex Cappy.

“We’ve been seeing phenomenal growth across the UK and Ireland, so we know there’s a huge opportunity to take the business further here, and Europe more broadly is of particular interest to us.”

A significant focus of the new capital will be deepening First Table’s presence in the UK and Ireland, strengthening relationships with restaurant partners, and giving diners and restaurants more ways to use the platform. The raise will also support growing awareness in the company’s other core markets, including New Zealand, where First Table was founded in 2014.

“A big part of this raise is about going deeper in the markets where we’re seeing the strongest momentum, and the UK and Ireland are leading that charge,” Cappy said.

“That means bringing more value to our restaurant partners and diners, and creating more opportunities for the hospitality industry to thrive.”

Unlike most booking platforms, First Table charges restaurants nothing. Diners pay a small booking fee, and venues list for free.

“An empty table at 5.30pm is revenue a restaurant never gets back,” Cappy said. “We help to turn those empty seats into paying customers, and the diner gets a meal they might not have booked otherwise. Everyone wins.”

The company is seeing strong demand across the UK and Ireland, with bookings tripling over the past two years despite a prolonged squeeze on consumer spending.

“People are being cautious with how they spend their money right now, but we know they still want to go out and connect over a meal, and the benefit that we offer at First Table is really appealing,” Cappy said.

“Equally, it has been a tough time for hospitality, and First Table gives restaurants another way to get diners through the door and build a buzz during usually quiet times.”

First Table has now seated more than five million diners globally since launching in Queenstown, New Zealand in 2014, and today operates in over 65 cities across New Zealand, Australia, the UK and Ireland, connecting 3.9 million-plus diners with over 5,000 restaurants worldwide, with the UK and Ireland now its fastest-growing region.

item.dc:creator: Staff Reporter
item.description:
UK head-quartered advisory firm LAVA Advisory Partners has appointed veteran M&A executives Carlo Porreca and Helen Dixon as its first Partners based outside the UK. Their arrival marks the launch of LAVA’s permanent US presence, with the firm establishing an office in New York’s iconic Chrysler Building. LAVA is a London-based middle-market M&A advisory firm […]

The post Carlo Porreca and Helen Dixon join UK head-quartered firm LAVA as it opens New York office appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
UK head-quartered advisory firm LAVA Advisory Partners has appointed veteran M&A executives Carlo Porreca and Helen Dixon as its first Partners based outside the UK. Their arrival marks the launch of LAVA’s permanent US presence, with the firm establishing an office in New York’s iconic Chrysler Building.

LAVA is a London-based middle-market M&A advisory firm with an existing track record working with US private equity. The US expansion enables the firm to act as a concierge for American private equity and investment firms seeking acquisitions and investments across the UK and Europe.

The US expansion follows LAVA’s recent $10.7 million (£8 million) growth funding agreement with Beechbrook Capital, and their presence in the market will be supported by Porreca and Dixon’s extensive relationships and experience within the private equity space.

Porreca brings nearly two decades of experience in deal origination, investment banking, private equity origination, and M&A. The founder of Wall Springs Capital, he will lead LAVA’s US sponsor coverage, with a particular focus on B2B, healthcare, and technology-enabled services.

Dixon has more than 20 years’ transaction advisory experience and has held senior roles at Grant Thornton and BDO. Originally from the UK and based in the US since 2017, she specializes in financial due diligence and will work across LAVA’s international transactions.

Simon Woodcock, Partner at LAVA Advisory Partners, said: “We already work regularly with US investors, and having Carlo and Helen in the market means those relationships can become a much more seamless part of our work. We really believe our unique approach will resonate with the US market Carlo and Helen know so well, and I’m excited for what’s ahead.”

Carlo Porreca, Partner at LAVA Advisory Partners, said: “I’ve spent much of my career connecting business owners with investors, often across different markets. LAVA’s deep understanding of the UK and European business landscape, combined with my US sponsor relationships and knowledge, gives us an unprecedented opportunity to put the most relevant opportunities in front of the right people, for the best possible results.”

Helen Dixon, Partner at LAVA Advisory Partners, said: “Having spent much of my career working across UK and US transactions, I’ve seen first-hand how differently buyers in each market can assess opportunities and approach a transaction. I’m excited to bring that perspective to LAVA’s cross-border work, helping our clients anticipate how they will be viewed by international investors and ensuring they are positioned to make the most of those opportunities.”

item.title: North-West London leading the UK’s new Industrial Revolution
item.dc:creator: Marco Callegari
item.description:
Base One, a science and technology hub in North Acton, has launched today offering a blueprint for the growth of advanced manufacturing in Britain by supporting high-growth scientific companies to scale in the UK. Howard Dawber, Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth, welcomed the launch, saying West London was fast becoming a leading […]

The post North-West London leading the UK’s new Industrial Revolution appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
Base One, a science and technology hub in North Acton, has launched today offering a blueprint for the growth of advanced manufacturing in Britain by supporting high-growth scientific companies to scale in the UK.

Howard Dawber, Deputy Mayor of London for Business and Growth, welcomed the launch, saying West London was fast becoming a leading centre for science, technology and advanced manufacturing, “By giving pioneering companies the affordable, flexible space they need to move from research and development to production, Base One will help more businesses start, grow and scale in London—creating good jobs, attracting investment and supporting a new era of British manufacturing, as we build a better, more prosperous London for everyone.”

The 55,000 sq ft site, formerly known as 1 Portal Way, has been developed by specialist developer and operator Sciopolis in partnership with Imperial College London. It offers 24 ready-to-occupy CL2 laboratories and 29 flexible offices, following an 11-month retrofit for biotech, cleantech and advanced materials startups moving from R&D into early-stage manufacturing.

Base One is designed to plug a gap that has long frustrated UK deep tech founders: the lack of affordable, flexible space that can scale with a company as it moves from lab bench to factory floor. The hub sits within Imperial’s Old Oak Innovation Cluster, one of four anchor sites in WestTech London, the university’s wider West London innovation ecosystem.

It also sits next door to Grapht Works, Imperial’s dedicated advanced manufacturing facility for pilot, demo and commercial-scale production meaning tenants can, in theory, move from prototyping to manufacturing without leaving the postcode.

Third tenant signs on

As it opens, Base One has confirmed its third occupier: Nanomox, an Imperial spinout that has developed a low-energy process for producing high-transparency zinc oxide, used in mineral sunscreens, cosmetics, rubber and electronics.

Nanomox joins two existing tenants already manufacturing on site, women’s intimate health brand P.Happi®, which is stocked in Boots and makes microbiome-focused products, and Ki 13, a cleantech company that has built a process for converting biomass into green hydrogen and biogenic CO2 for use in sustainable fuels.

Dr Francisco Malaret, founder and chief executive of Nanomox, said Base One was the only site in London that let the company begin manufacturing while staying inside an ecosystem suited to its stage of growth.

Ki 13 co-founder and chief executive Koji Muto said the North Acton location gave the company the accessibility, affordability and flexibility it needed as it scales out of the lab and into hardware engineering.

Part of a bigger regeneration push

Base One’s location is no accident. It borders Park Royal, London’s largest industrial estate and employer of more than 40,000 people, and sits within the Old Oak regeneration zone billed as the largest such opportunity in the capital. The area is set to be transformed by the arrival of Old Oak Common station, which will link HS2, the Elizabeth line and GWR services, putting it within reach of innovation clusters in Birmingham, Bristol, Oxford and Cambridge.

Imperial president Hugh Brady said Base One strengthened the UK’s network of national innovation assets and pointed to the university’s existing links with manufacturing and research hubs elsewhere in the country, including the West Midlands, Harwell, Oxford, Bristol and Cardiff.

Sciopolis chief executive Charlie Mitchell said high-growth companies had struggled for too long to find the space they need to scale in the UK, and described Base One and the wider cluster as a blueprint for advanced manufacturing in Britain.

Sciopolis said it plans to build a network of similar sites across other UK innovation clusters.

The post North-West London leading the UK’s new Industrial Revolution appeared first on UKTN.

item.title: Itoflow secures £1.8m to build AI agents for investor portfolio management
item.dc:creator: Kirstie Pickering
item.description:
Itoflow, an AI platform helping professional investment teams scale research and portfolio management, has raised $2.5m (£1.8m) in pre-seed funding. Founded in 2026, Itoflow is building AI agents that learn how each investment firm researches opportunities, manages risk and reviews portfolios.  Itoflow says the platform does not impose a particular investment philosophy – instead, it turns […]

The post Itoflow secures £1.8m to build AI agents for investor portfolio management appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
Itoflow, an AI platform helping professional investment teams scale research and portfolio management, has raised $2.5m (£1.8m) in pre-seed funding.

Founded in 2026, Itoflow is building AI agents that learn how each investment firm researches opportunities, manages risk and reviews portfolios. 

Itoflow says the platform does not impose a particular investment philosophy – instead, it turns each team’s own approach into governed workflows that can operate continuously across global markets and asset classes, including equities, bonds, ETFs, commodities and digital assets. 

The startup says its agentic infrastructure gives Itoflow greater control over the security and reliability of agents designed to operate for months or years as markets change.

In current pilots, investment teams define the investment approach, risk constraints and review criteria they want Itoflow to apply. 

Its AI agents then use those instructions to conduct quantitative research and backtesting, continuously monitor portfolios and surface material changes with supporting evidence. This enables teams to research and review more investments, monitor more portfolios and apply their processes more consistently without building a significantly larger quantitative research function.

The pre-seed round was led by Balderton Capital and included angel investors such as Cleo founder, Barney Hussey-Yeo. 

Itoflow will use the funding to expand its engineering and quantitative research teams, accelerate product development and support its commercial and regulatory work.

“Our long-term research goal is to build self-improving investment agents,” says Aditya Jha, co-founder and CEO of Itoflow. 

“As an agent supports a mandate over months and years, it should learn which approaches continue to hold up, identify promising new signals and recognise when an apparent edge has decayed. Within the parameters set by each investment team, these agents could become a powerful tool for continuous discovery.”

Embedd’s platform creates a digital twin of chips and uses AI agents to generate the integration code engineers would otherwise write by hand. The startup says the approach lets manufacturers ship production-ready […]

The post Embedd raises £2m to accelerate infrastructure for physical AI appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
London-based Embedd has raised $2.7m (£2m) to develop its build capabilities of infrastructure for physical AI and expand its work with semiconductor partners.

Embedd’s platform creates a digital twin of chips and uses AI agents to generate the integration code engineers would otherwise write by hand. The startup says the approach lets manufacturers ship production-ready chip software up to six times faster. 

Ukrainian founders Michael Lazarenko, Maxim Gorinov and Valentin Gololobov were running a hardware company when Covid-era shortages forced them to source whatever chips they could find and rewrite their software from scratch each time. 

Each new chip meant weeks of manual integration work. Russia’s invasion of Ukraine disrupted their supply chain again – and this pattern convinced them the problem would only get worse as physical AI scales.

Seedcamp, the lead investor of the pre-seed round, says intelligent machines are built using chips from dozens of different manufacturers, and none of them are able to communicate with each other. Wiring them up means engineers writing pages of custom integration code for every single chip by hand – and this is the bottleneck Embedd is building to solve.

In addition to Seedcamp, the round also included participation from Cocoa, Connect Ventures, 2100 Ventures, Vesna Capital, U.ventures, Underline Ventures, Common Magic and Roosh Ventures.

“The next wave of AI will power factories, vehicles, robots and critical infrastructure, but today, every change in hardware creates huge complexity for software teams and that friction is already massively slowing innovation,” says Lazarenko. 

“We built Embedd to address exactly that, and we’re thrilled to have the backing of Seedcamp as we scale.”

The post Embedd raises £2m to accelerate infrastructure for physical AI appeared first on UKTN.

item.title: UK and Ukraine sign landmark AI deal to develop new technologies
item.dc:creator: Kirstie Pickering
item.description:
A landmark AI deal between the UK and Ukraine has been signed as the two countries join forces to develop new technology and military capabilities. Bringing together Britain’s AI ecosystem with Ukraine’s operational experience, engineering talent and technological innovation, the new deal will enable access to Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs database. The platform provides real […]

The post UK and Ukraine sign landmark AI deal to develop new technologies appeared first on UKTN.
item.content:encoded:
A landmark AI deal between the UK and Ukraine has been signed as the two countries join forces to develop new technology and military capabilities.

Bringing together Britain’s AI ecosystem with Ukraine’s operational experience, engineering talent and technological innovation, the new deal will enable access to Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs database.

The platform provides real world data and insights to train AI models, collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the battlefield in Ukraine.

These sensors and cameras capture millions of objects, such as tanks, artillery, air defence systems, infantry and aerial targets, feeding back data to the Avengers Lab to train new AI models.

The deal will first focus on defence and national security, bringing together engineers, academics, businesses and military operational expertise from both countries to act as an AI cell to solve key national security challenges for both countries.

The government says Avengers AI Labs will give British innovators and researchers unparalleled access to real-world operational insights and the opportunity to ‘plug and play’.

In return, the UK will back Ukraine with its universities, researchers, technology companies and AI ecosystem, allowing Ukraine to draw on British expertise to accelerate the development of solutions to urgent challenges. The UK also hopes to transform operational experience and unique datasets into technologies with long-term benefits for both countries.

As part of the agreement, pilot projects will take place with three British startups – Bristol’s Sintela, Oxford’s Mind Foundry and London’s Skyral.

The first of the trial technologies will be rolled out at a UK defence site to protect bases from protestors and hostile actors trying to gain intelligence.

The project, which uses Ukrainian data and UK technology, turns buried fibre-optic cables into a giant AI-enabled sensor. As well as military bases, the technology could be used to protect airports, prisons, railways and energy plants in the future.

The second project will see the UK and Ukraine explore the development of next-generation low-power AI chips designed to power future drones, robotics and autonomous systems.

“This groundbreaking partnership will bring together Ukraine’s unrivalled operational experience with Britain’s world-class AI ecosystem, giving us the opportunity to develop the technologies of the future, changing lives here in Britain and saving lives on the battlefield in Ukraine,” says Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

“By combining Ukrainian battlefield data with British expertise, we will accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security, but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home.”
